title: Linear First-Order Equations & the Integrating Factor

questions.q: Write $y' + 2xy = x$ in the standard form $y' + P(x)y = Q(x)$ and identify $P(x)$ and $Q(x)$.
Is $y' = \dfrac{y}{x} + x^2$ linear? Rewrite it in standard form.
questions.answer: Yes. Standard form: $y' - \dfrac{1}{x}y = x^2$, so $P(x) = -\dfrac{1}{x}$, $Q(x) = x^2$.

questions.q: Is $y' = y^2 + x$ a linear first-order equation? Justify your answer.
questions.answer: No. A linear equation cannot contain $y^2$ or any other nonlinear function of $y$; the dependent variable and its derivatives must appear only to the first power and never multiplied together.

questions.q: Write $xy' + 3y = \sin x$ ($x>0$) in standard form.
Find the integrating factor for $y' + 3y = e^x$.
Find the integrating factor for $y' - \dfrac{2}{x}y = x$, $x>0$.
Find the integrating factor for $y' + \dfrac{1}{x}y = 3x$, $x>0$.
Find the integrating factor for $y' + 2xy = 4x$.
Solve $y' + 3y = e^x$.
Solve $y' - \dfrac{2}{x}y = x$, $x>0$.
Solve $y' + \dfrac{1}{x}y = 3x$, $x>0$.
Solve $y' + 2xy = 4x$.

questions.answer: With $\mu = e^x$: $(e^xy)' = 2e^x$, so $e^xy = 2e^x + C$, giving $y = 2 + Ce^{-x}$. Since $y(0)=0$, $C=-2$: $y = 2 - 2e^{-x}$.
With $\mu=e^{-x}$: $(e^{-x}y)'=e^{x}$, so $e^{-x}y=e^x+C$, giving $y=e^{2x}+Ce^{x}$. Since $y(0)=3$: $1+C=3 \Rightarrow C=2$. So $y=e^{2x}+2e^{x}$.

questions.q: Solve $y'+\dfrac{2}{x}y=\dfrac{\cos x}{x^2}$, $x>0$, $y(\pi)=0$.
questions.answer: With $\mu=x^2$: $(x^2y)'=\cos x$, so $x^2y=\sin x+C$. Since $y(\pi)=0$: $\pi^2(0)=\sin\pi+C \Rightarrow C=0$. So $y=\dfrac{\sin x}{x^2}$.

questions.q: A tank starts with $100$ L of pure water. Brine with concentration $2$ kg/L flows in at $3$ L/min, and the well-mixed solution flows out at the same rate. If $Q(t)$ is the salt (kg) at time $t$, the balance gives $Q' = 6 - 0.03Q$. Solve for $Q(t)$ given $Q(0)=0$.
For the tank above, what is the long-run (as $t\to\infty$) salt content, and why does that match the tank's incoming brine concentration times its volume?
questions.answer: As $t\to\infty$, $e^{-0.03t}\to0$, so $Q(t)\to200$ kg. This matches $2$ kg/L $\times\,100$ L $=200$ kg — once the transient dies out, the tank equilibrates to the same concentration as the inflow.

questions.q: An RL circuit with resistance $R$, inductance $L$, and constant EMF $E_0$ satisfies $L\dfrac{dI}{dt}+RI=E_0$. Rewrite this in standard linear form and identify its integrating factor.
Solve the RL circuit equation from above for $I(t)$ given $I(0)=0$.
Explain why every first-order linear equation $y'+P(x)y=Q(x)$ can, in principle, be solved by the integrating-factor method, regardless of the specific $P$ and $Q$.
questions.answer: The integrating factor $\mu(x)=e^{\int P(x)\,dx}$ is built directly from $P$, and by construction $\mu' = P\mu$, so $(\mu y)' = \mu y' + \mu' y = \mu(y'+Py) = \mu Q$. Integrating both sides always gives $\mu y = \int \mu Q\,dx + C$ — the method never fails structurally, though the resulting integral may not have an elementary closed form.

questions.q: Solve $y' - 4y = 8x$.
Solve $\cos x\,y' + \sin x\,y = 1$ for $-\frac{\pi}{2}<x<\frac{\pi}{2}$. (Divide by $\cos x$ first, and recognize the integrating factor without computing an integral.)
questions.answer: Standard form: $y' + \tan x\,y = \sec x$. Here $\mu = e^{\int \tan x\,dx}=e^{-\ln|\cos x|}=\sec x$ (or note directly that $\mu=\sec x$ makes $(\sec x\,y)'=\sec x\,y'+\sec x\tan x\,y$, matching the equation after multiplying by $\sec x$). Then $(\sec x\,y)'=\sec^2x$, so $\sec x\,y=\tan x+C$, giving $y=\sin x+C\cos x$.

sections.heading: Comparing linear equations with separable equations

questions.q: The equation $y' = xy$ is both separable and linear (with $Q(x)=0$ — a homogeneous linear equation). Solve it using the integrating-factor method and confirm it matches the separable-equation approach.
questions.answer: Standard form: $y'-xy=0$, so $\mu=e^{-\int x\,dx}=e^{-x^2/2}$. Then $(e^{-x^2/2}y)'=0$, so $e^{-x^2/2}y=C$, giving $y=Ce^{x^2/2}$ — the same family obtained by separating variables directly.

questions.q: For which choice(s) of $Q(x)$ does a linear equation $y'+P(x)y=Q(x)$ reduce to a separable equation in general? Explain.
questions.answer: When $Q(x)=0$ (the homogeneous case): the equation becomes $y'=-P(x)y$, which separates as $\dfrac{dy}{y}=-P(x)\,dx$. For nonzero $Q(x)$, the equation is linear but generally not separable, since $y'$ would depend on both $x$ and $y$ in a way that can't be split into a product of single-variable factors.

questions.q: A linear equation $y'+P(x)y=Q(x)$ has general solution $y=x^2+\dfrac{C}{x}$. Given that $P(x)=\dfrac{1}{x}$, find $Q(x)$.
questions.answer: Differentiate: $y'=2x-\dfrac{C}{x^2}$. Then $y'+\dfrac{1}{x}y = 2x-\dfrac{C}{x^2}+\dfrac{1}{x}\left(x^2+\dfrac{C}{x}\right)=2x-\dfrac{C}{x^2}+x+\dfrac{C}{x^2}=3x$. So $Q(x)=3x$ (consistent with the earlier integrating-factor question above).
